html:
The Tulip Revolution was a wave of protests in Kyrgyzstan in March 2005 that drove out President Askar Akayev, who had led the country since 1990, before independence. It followed disputed parliamentary elections in February and March.

Protests began in the south, in Jalal-Abad and Osh, where opposition supporters took over government buildings. On 24 March crowds in the capital, Bishkek, stormed the seat of government, and Akayev fled to Kazakhstan and then Russia; he signed his resignation in April. Looting followed in Bishkek that night. The name echoed the colour revolutions in Georgia in 2003 and Ukraine in 2004.

Kurmanbek Bakiyev, an opposition leader from the south, became president, but his rule also turned corrupt, and another uprising in April 2010 ousted him after deadly shooting in Bishkek; ethnic violence in Osh followed that June. A third upheaval came in 2020. Control of the Kumtor gold mine was one of the prizes in these struggles. Compare the peaceful Mongolian revolution of 1990.
sum: The Tulip Revolution was a wave of protests in Kyrgyzstan in March 2005 that drove out President Askar Akayev, who had led the country since 1990, before independence. It followed disputed parliamentary elections in February and March.
